claims.claim: One process: the index lives in memory once. Threads easily handle ~100 req/s bursts.
claims.about: Flask served by waitress, one process with 8 threads
claims.measured: Flask with threads (gthread) reached 4,031 req/s plaintext and 3,777 req/s JSON on 1 CPU; sync Flask reached 1,732 / 1,700 req/s
claims.why: Threaded Flask on one CPU measured roughly 17 to 40 times the claimed 100 req/s, so 'easily' holds (waitress itself was not measured, but threaded Flask on another WSGI server was).

claims.claim: It should meet the 50 ms target
claims.about: Flask service handling lookups on Python
claims.measured: python-flask-gthread p99 37.24 ms plaintext and 37.73 ms JSON with the CPU saturated at about 4,000 req/s; python-flask p99 about 51 ms at about 1,700 req/s
claims.why: Even with the CPU saturated, threaded Flask's p99 is under 50 ms, and at 100 req/s it is far from saturation, so framework overhead should not break the target for single-variant lookups (large region responses are not covered).

claims.claim: The server starts straight away and loads the index in a background thread
claims.why: Flask servers measured at roughly 0.6 to 1 s to start, which fits 'straight away' compared with the 3-minute index load.

claims.claim: A single process matters because the 4 GB index would otherwise be duplicated per worker
claims.why: The benchmarks only measure small per-server memory with no large in-process data, and each container had 1 CPU, so per-worker duplication of a 4 GB structure cannot be checked.

claims.claim: A lookup is a binary search (microseconds) instead of a scan over every variant
claims.why: No benchmark measures numpy binary-search time or scans over a large array.

claims.claim: The per-chromosome split makes copies of the arrays, which could add up to roughly another 4 GB at load time
claims.about: Python/numpy memory use during index load
claims.why: The benchmarks do not cover memory for copying large numpy arrays.
